issues.title: Relays drop the GNU overhead when a message passes through more than three towers

checks.done_when: A message sent from Ankh-Morpork to Genua over the eight towers of the coast line arrives with the X-Clacks-Overhead field exactly as the sending tower set it: the same value, in the same position in the header, with no extra spaces and no second copy of the field. This holds when the message is rerouted by the Hub after it has left the first tower, when it waits at any tower during fog and is sent on later, when a tower on the way restarts while the message is in its queue, and when a tower on the way still speaks the old signal box protocol, as the three Lancre towers do. A message that arrives at a tower with an empty overhead value is passed on with the empty value kept, not dropped and not replaced, because that is what the Quirm towers send after a restart. A message that arrives with no overhead field at all is passed on without one. None of these cases writes a warning to the tower log, and the relay's log line for a hop shows the overhead it copied at debug level only.
checks.proven_by: cargo nextest run -p clacks-network overhead_survives_eight_towers overhead_survives_reroute overhead_survives_fog overhead_survives_restart overhead_survives_signal_box

checks.done_when: A message that passes through four towers keeps its overhead.
The relay copies the overhead in its send step, so every route, including a reroute by the Hub, passes through the copy. The receive step no longer touches the field.
checks.proven_by: cargo nextest run -p clacks-relay send_step_copies_overhead; grep shows no write to the overhead field in receive.rs

checks.done_when: An empty overhead value is passed on as an empty value. The copy code treats an empty string and a missing field as two different cases, and each has its own test, because the Quirm towers send an empty value for the first hour after a restart and a change that merged the two cases would drop the field for exactly those towers.
checks.proven_by: cargo nextest run -p clacks-relay empty_overhead_kept missing_overhead_not_added

checks.done_when: A message with no overhead field is passed on without one; no tower adds the network default.

The three Lancre towers that still speak the old signal box protocol pass the overhead on as well. Their path keeps the old copy function, which now has a test of its own, and a comment above it names clacks#247 as the issue that retires it together with the protocol.

The relay's log line for a hop shows the overhead at debug level and is absent at info. At info a tower's log grows by no more lines per message than it did before the change, measured over an hour of the recorded Ankh-Morpork traffic replayed through a test tower.
checks.proven_by: scripts/replay-traffic --line ankh-morpork --hours 1 --level info, then compare line counts with the run on main; the counts must match to the line

checks.done_when: No setting turns the copy off on any tower.
checks.proven_by: grep for overhead in the tower config schema finds no key

checks.done_when: A tower that restarts while a message waits in its queue sends the message on with its overhead after the restart. The queue file written before the restart and read after it keeps the field, and a queue file written by the version before this change, which has no field for it, is read without an error and its messages are sent on without an overhead.
checks.proven_by: cargo nextest run -p clacks-relay queue_survives_restart queue_reads_old_format; the old-format queue file is checked in under tests/data/queue-0.3.bin

checks.done_when: Messages already sent without their overhead are left as they are; the change only affects messages sent after it is deployed, and the release note says so in one line.
checks.proven_by: CHANGELOG.md has the line under 0.4; no migration in the pull request

checks.done_when: The end-to-end run on the test network sends 200 messages from Ankh-Morpork to Genua with fog on two towers and a restart on one, and every message arrives with its overhead. The run takes under four minutes, so it stays in the default test suite.
checks.proven_by: cargo nextest run -p clacks-network e2e_coast_line --run-ignored all; the run time is printed at the end and must be under 240 s on the test machine

checks.done_when: The operators' handbook page on headers says the overhead is kept on every hop.

points.text: No test for an empty overhead value. The Quirm towers send one after a restart, and the copy code treats it apart from a missing field.
points.reply: Added empty_overhead_kept; it fails on the branch and I am fixing the copy.

points.text: The new log line for each hop is at info, which adds about 40,000 lines a day on the Ankh-Morpork line.

issues.title: Tower status page shows a relay as up for a minute after its shutters jam

checks.done_when: Tower status page shows a relay as up for a minute after its shutters jam: the case the issue describes no longer happens on the test network.

A test that fails on main and passes on the branch shows the change for clacks#215. It runs in the default suite, starts real tower processes rather than calling the changed function directly, and finishes in under a minute on the test machine, so it is not marked ignored.

The status page shows the change for every tower on the line, checked against the Ankh-Morpork to Sto Lat line in the test network, and the page still loads in under a second with all 112 towers listed.
checks.proven_by: npm run e2e -- status-page; the timing is printed per page load

checks.done_when: Nothing changes for the three Lancre towers that still speak the old signal box protocol: their traffic before and after the change is the same, message for message, over an hour of recorded traffic.
checks.proven_by: scripts/replay-traffic --line lancre --hours 1 on main and on the branch, then diff the two outputs; the diff must be empty

checks.done_when: Tower config written by 0.3 is read without an error and keeps every setting it had. A new key added by this change has a default that leaves a tower behaving as it does today, so a tower that is not upgraded and a tower that is upgraded but not configured send the same traffic.
checks.proven_by: cargo nextest run -p clacks-config reads_0_3_config default_keeps_behaviour

checks.done_when: The operators' handbook names the change on the page operators read for it.

A tower that restarts in the middle of the change's work picks it up again where it stopped, with no message lost and none sent twice. This is checked with a restart at each of the points where the relay writes its queue file, not only at the start and the end.
The change adds no log line at info level. At debug, each new line names the tower, the line and the message id, so an operator can follow one message through the log.
checks.proven_by: grep the diff for info! and warn!; read the debug lines in review

checks.done_when: Let the Hub pause one line without stopping the whole network: the case the issue describes no longer happens on the test network.

A test that fails on main and passes on the branch shows the change for clacks#198. It runs in the default suite, starts real tower processes rather than calling the changed function directly, and finishes in under a minute on the test machine, so it is not marked ignored.

The status page shows the change for every tower on the line, checked against the Ankh-Morpork to Sto Lat line in the test network, and the page still loads in under a second with all 112 towers listed.

checks.done_when: Tower config written by 0.3 is read without an error and keeps every setting it had. A new key added by this change has a default that leaves a tower behaving as it does today, so a tower that is not upgraded and a tower that is upgraded but not configured send the same traffic.

A tower that restarts in the middle of the change's work picks it up again where it stopped, with no message lost and none sent twice. This is checked with a restart at each of the points where the relay writes its queue file, not only at the start and the end.

decisions.question: Which towers does the fix cover: every tower, or only those on lines longer than three hops?
options: Only towers on lines longer than three hops
decisions.reason: The overhead is dropped in the relay code that every tower runs, and nothing in it is specific to long lines. Fixing it only on long lines would need a second code path and would leave the bug in place for the day a short line grows a fourth tower.

decisions.question: How many towers should the end-to-end test send a message through?
decisions.reason: Four is the smallest count that shows the bug, but the Ankh-Morpork to Genua line has eight towers and is the longest in use. Eight covers both without making the test slower than the rest of the suite; twelve added forty seconds and covered no line that exists.

decisions.question: Should messages already sent without their overhead be repaired, or left as they are?
options: Repair them from the sending tower's log
Leave them and fix only new messages
decisions.reason: The sending tower's log keeps the overhead for seven days, so a repair is possible, but it means rewriting messages that operators may already have read out. Leaving them affects about 300 messages a day until the fix ships, and none of them carry anything but the header. A repair can be its own issue if the Hub wants one.

decisions.question: Which header field should carry the overhead across a hop?
options: A new field in the relay envelope
decisions.reason: Every tower already reads X-Clacks-Overhead; the bug is that the relay forgets to copy it. A new envelope field would need every tower upgraded at once.

decisions.question: Where should the regression test live?
options: In the relay crate's own tests
In the network tests that start real towers
decisions.reason: The bug only shows when a message crosses real tower processes. The relay crate's tests call the copy function directly and passed the whole time the bug was in place.

decisions.question: What should a tower do with an incoming message that has no overhead at all?
options: Add the overhead from the network default
decisions.reason: Some private lines never set the overhead, and adding one would change messages the sender wrote. Refusing them would break those lines today over a header nobody on them asked for.

decisions.question: Copy the overhead in the relay's receive step or its send step?
decisions.reason: The send step already builds the outgoing envelope and is the one place every route passes through. Copying in the receive step would miss messages the Hub reroutes after they arrive, which is how the fourth-tower case loses it.

decisions.question: Keep the old copy function for the signal box protocol, or remove it?
options: Keep it until the old protocol is retired
decisions.reason: Three towers on the Lancre line still speak the old signal box protocol, and that path uses the old function. Removing it would need those towers moved first, which is clacks#247.

decisions.question: Should the fix ship behind a setting so a tower can turn it off?
decisions.reason: A setting would let one tower drop the overhead again, which is the bug. The change copies one field and has a test across eight towers; if it misbehaves, reverting the commit is quicker than finding which towers turned a setting off.

decisions.question: Is the missing test for an empty overhead value a blocking point?
decisions.reason: An empty value is what the Quirm towers send after a restart, and the copy code treats an empty string and a missing field differently. Without a test the next change to that code can bring the bug back for exactly those towers.

decisions.question: Accept the new log line on every hop at info, or ask for it at debug level?
decisions.reason: At info the line adds one log entry per hop per message, about 40,000 a day on the Ankh-Morpork line alone, and tower logs are already the reason clacks#246 exists.

decisions.question: Over what window should a tower's message rate be measured?
decisions.reason: A minute swings with every long message and would make the Hub reroute on noise. Fifteen minutes is longer than most fog delays last, so a slow tower would have recovered before the Hub noticed. Five matches how often operators look at the status page.

decisions.question: Should the rate count words or messages?
decisions.reason: A tower's speed is set by how many shutter frames it sends, which follows words. Counting messages would make a tower that sends long reports look slow and one that sends short acknowledgements look fast.

decisions.question: What rate counts as slow enough to route around?
decisions.reason: Lines differ by a factor of four in speed, so a fixed number would route around every tower on the Lancre line and none on the Ankh-Morpork one. Half the median follows each line's own speed with no setting to keep up to date. Operators can still pause a line by hand.

decisions.question: Where should the rate be stored?
decisions.reason: The status page already reads the tower status table, so the rate shows there with no new query, and it survives a Hub restart.

decisions.question: Should the status page show the rate?
decisions.reason: When the Hub routes around a tower, operators need to see why, or they will think the tower is down and send someone up it.

decisions.question: Route around a slow tower at once, or after it stays slow for a while?
options: After two windows in a row
decisions.reason: A single slow window is often one long message. Waiting for two windows in a row costs at most ten minutes and avoids rerouting traffic back and forth every five.

decisions.question: How many checks should the plan have for the routing change?
options: Routing, status page and the restart case
decisions.reason: The rate is used in three places, and the restart case is where a rate kept only in memory would have been lost. Leaving the status page out of the plan would let its column ship empty.

decisions.question: Which order counts as right after fog lifts?
options: The order messages arrived at the tower
decisions.reason: Operators already send urgent messages first by hand when a line comes back; the bug is that the relay ignores arrival order within a priority. Plain arrival order would hold an urgent message behind a morning of routine traffic.

decisions.question: Should the fix cover messages that waited at more than one fogged tower?
decisions.reason: Fog on the Lancre line often covers two or three towers at once, and that is the case operators reported. A fix for one tower would leave the reported case broken.

decisions.question: Sort the queue when fog lifts, or keep it sorted as messages arrive?
decisions.reason: Keeping it sorted costs a little on every insert but means the queue is always ready. Sorting when fog lifts adds a pause of up to two seconds on a long queue, at the moment the line is needed.

decisions.question: Use the message's arrival time or its queue position to break a tie?
decisions.reason: Tower clocks drift (clacks#234), so two messages can carry the same or reversed times. The queue position is assigned by the tower itself and cannot be wrong.

decisions.question: What should happen to a queue longer than the shutters can clear in an hour?
options: Send the first hour and ask the Hub about the rest
Drop routine messages older than a day
decisions.reason: Dropping messages is a decision for the Hub, not the relay, and asking the Hub adds a step nobody is awake to answer at night. Sending in order clears the longest queue seen this year in about three hours, which operators said is acceptable.

decisions.question: Is the round 1 point about the missing fog test answered?
decisions.reason: The new test fogs three towers, queues messages of two priorities and checks the order at the far end, which is the case the point asked for.

decisions.question: Which light reading should switch the lamps?
decisions.reason: Every tower in 0.4 has its own sensor, and the nearest weather station can be a valley away, in different light.

decisions.question: At what reading should the lamps switch on?
options: The level operators set by hand today
decisions.reason: Operators have tuned the level per tower over years, for the hills behind each one. A fixed level would undo that tuning on the first night.

decisions.question: Keep the clock as a fallback when a sensor fails?
decisions.reason: A failed sensor reads zero, which would leave the lamps on all day, or full, which would leave them off all night. The clock is wrong by up to an hour but never by twelve.

decisions.question: Should the change reach the towers on the Überwald line, which have older lamp controllers?
options: No, leave them on the clock
decisions.reason: The older controllers have no input for a sensor, and replacing them is hardware work the agents cannot do or test. Leaving those six towers on the clock keeps them as they are today; the plan says so, so it is not mistaken for a bug later.

decisions.question: How many times should the driver retry a failed frame?
decisions.reason: Most failed frames are a gust of wind and clear on the first or second try; the logs show none that cleared after the fourth. Five leaves room and still frees the line within a few seconds.

decisions.question: What should happen to a frame that still fails after the last retry?
options: Hold the message and tell the operator
Skip the frame and send the rest
decisions.reason: A message with a missing frame can change meaning, and the receiving tower cannot tell. Holding it costs one message, and the operator decides.

decisions.question: Should the retry count be a setting?
decisions.reason: The towers on the Genua coast fail more frames in sea wind than inland ones, and their operators asked to tune this. A per-tower setting is one value in the existing tower config.

decisions.question: Block on the missing migration for messages already billed twice?
options: Block until a migration is added
Pass, and file the migration as its own issue
decisions.reason: The fix stops new double counts and its tests show it. Correcting past invoices touches money already collected and needs the Hub's say on refunds, which no agent can give; it is a separate piece of work with its own owner.

decisions.question: Report a jam from the shutter driver directly, or wait for the next health check?
options: Wait for the next health check
Report it from the driver at once
decisions.reason: The health check runs once a minute, which is the delay the issue is about. The driver already knows the moment a shutter jams and can mark the tower down in the status table itself.
